sections.heading: What are Shortest Path Algorithms?
sections.content: A shortest path problem asks for the cheapest way to get from one node to another in a graph whose edges have costs (weights), such as distance, time, price or risk. BFS already solves this when every edge costs the same. Once edges have different weights you need a different tool: Dijkstra for non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford when weights can be negative or the number of edges is limited, Floyd-Warshall for all pairs, and 0-1 BFS when weights are only 0 or 1. All of them rely on one idea called relaxation: if going through node u gives a shorter route to v, update the best known distance to v.

sections.heading: When to Use It
items: Find the cheapest, fastest or shortest route between nodes in a weighted graph
Compute the distance from one source to every other node (single-source)
Find shortest paths between every pair of nodes (all-pairs)
Route with a limit on the number of stops or edges
Detect negative cycles (currency arbitrage, impossible constraints)
Minimize the largest edge on a path (effort, risk, bottleneck problems)
Count the number of shortest paths
Keywords: shortest, cheapest, minimum cost, minimum time, network delay, flights with K stops, maximum probability

sections.heading: The Core Idea: Relaxation
sections.content: Keep an array dist[] where dist[v] is the best distance found so far to v (infinity at the start, 0 at the source). For an edge u → v with weight w, if dist[u] + w < dist[v], you have found a shorter way to v, so you update dist[v] = dist[u] + w. That update is called relaxing the edge. Every shortest path algorithm is a different strategy for choosing the order in which edges are relaxed. Dijkstra picks the closest unfinished node each time, Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge repeatedly, and Floyd-Warshall relaxes through every possible middle node.

sections.heading: Why Dijkstra Fails With Negative Edges
sections.content: Dijkstra assumes that once the closest unfinished node is taken from the heap, no later path can reach it more cheaply, because every extra edge only adds cost. A negative edge breaks that assumption: a longer route could become cheaper after crossing the negative edge, but Dijkstra has already finalized the node. Use Bellman-Ford in that case.

Dijkstra Variants You Will See
items: Minimize the sum of weights: the standard version
Minimize the largest edge on the path (minimum effort, swim in rising water): replace d + w with max(d, w)
Maximize a product of probabilities: use a max heap and multiply instead of add
Count shortest paths: keep a ways[] array, copy ways on a strictly better distance and add ways on an equal distance
Extra state in the node (stops left, fuel, keys): make the state (node, extra) part of the heap entry and the dist table
Grid shortest path with costs per cell: treat each cell as a node and use the same structure

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
items: Using Dijkstra with negative edge weights (use Bellman-Ford)
Using plain BFS on a weighted graph, which counts edges instead of cost
Forgetting the stale-entry check (if d > dist[node] continue), which wastes time and can repeat work
Integer overflow when adding to Int.MAX_VALUE (check for unreachable first, or use Long)
Forgetting to add the edge in both directions for an undirected graph
In Bellman-Ford with a K-edge limit, updating dist in place so a round uses edges relaxed in the same round
Putting the k loop inside in Floyd-Warshall (k must be the outermost loop)
Treating the minimize-the-maximum problem as a sum problem
Using plain Dijkstra when the state has extra information such as stops left
Returning dist values of Int.MAX_VALUE as a real distance instead of reporting unreachable

sections.heading: Key Takeaways
items: Relaxation is the core step: update dist[v] when dist[u] + w is smaller
Use BFS for equal weights, 0-1 BFS for weights 0 and 1, Dijkstra for non-negative weights, and Bellman-Ford for negative weights
Dijkstra uses a min heap, finalizes the closest node each time, and skips stale heap entries
Bellman-Ford relaxes all edges V - 1 times and detects negative cycles with one extra pass
Limit on edges or stops: run Bellman-Ford rounds with a copied array, or add the count to the state
Variants change only the combine step: max for bottleneck paths, multiplication for probabilities, an extra array for counting paths
